title: Grove deters allocation to unapproved markets with a 100% capital charge rather than a prohibition
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.3.7.1.1.2.5.2 handles an unapproved market with a price rather than a rule: "Any allocation to the syrupUSDG/USDG market, which is not approved, is subject to a **100% CRR**."

Grove is not told it may not allocate there. It is told that if it does, the position must be backed one-for-one with capital — which strips out all leverage and therefore all economic point to the allocation. The prohibition is implemented as an economic dead end.

The technique has real advantages over a ban. It **degrades gracefully**: if the vault curator routes some funds to the unapproved market for reasons outside Grove's control, the outcome is an expensive position rather than a violation, so the framework stays coherent instead of being breached by circumstance. It is **self-enforcing**: no one has to detect and punish the allocation, because the capital charge applies automatically wherever the exposure lands. And it **prices rather than forbids**, leaving room for an allocation that is genuinely worth doing despite the charge.

It also fits the intermediated structure exactly. A prohibition needs someone capable of obeying it; here the allocating party is a vault curator outside Grove's authority. A capital charge needs no one's compliance — it is computed from the resulting exposure.

The general form is worth naming: where an actor cannot control an outcome but must bear its consequences, converting the rule from a permission into a price keeps the rule enforceable. The limit of the technique is that it only deters parties who bear the cost. It works here because Grove's own capital is charged; it would not work against a counterparty who is indifferent to Grove's balance sheet.
description: Rather than forbidding the syrupUSDG/USDG market, the Atlas makes any exposure to it fully capital-backed — the allocation stays permitted but its return on capital collapses to zero.
